items.title: Put either participant first

states.label: Ordinary order
states.sm: Sā tapē e le tama le puaʻa.
states.note: The action comes first, followed by the marked doer and the thing acted on.

states.label: Thing acted on first
states.sm: ʻO le puaʻa sā tapē e le tama.
states.note: The pig is presented first. The verb keeps the short form.

states.label: Doer first
states.sm: ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa.
states.note: The boy is presented first. The verb takes the long form here.

items.caption: The three printed forms have the same English. Short and long forms here follow tendencies; the two command rules remain the only exceptionless ones.

items.title: What has been put first?

data.question: Which part is at the head of this sentence?

prompts.sm: ʻO le teine sā tatala=ina le faitotoʻa.
prompts.why: The girl, who opened the door, has been put first.

prompts.sm: ʻO le leo o le pepe na lagona e le tina.
prompts.why: The whole phrase naming the voice travels to the front together.

prompts.sm: I le faʻatoʻaga sā gālue ai le tama.
prompts.why: The place phrase goes first, and *ai* points back to it from after the verb.

items.intro: Look at the whole phrase before the rest of the sentence begins.

items.title: Two orders for the same naming sentence

states.label: Naming part first
states.note: The naming part carries the presenting particle. The boy follows it.

states.label: The one being named first
states.sm: ʻO le tama ʻo se uō.
states.note: The boy carries the presenting particle because he comes first; the naming part keeps its own particle too.

items.caption: Both printed sentences say the same thing. The order is largely free, with the speaker and demonstrative exceptions explained above.
